t:
(a) In General.—The International Space Station represents a significant investment of national resources, and it is a facility that embodies a cooperative international approach to the exploration and utilization of space. As such, it is important that its continued viability and productivity be ensured, to the maximum extent possible, after the Space Shuttle is retired. 
    (b) Contingency Plan.—The Administrator shall develop a contingency plan and arrangements, including use of International Space Station international partner cargo resupply capabilities, to ensure the continued viability and productivity of the International Space Station in the event that United States commercial cargo resupply services are not available during any extended period after the date that the Space Shuttle is retired. The plan shall be delivered to the Committee on Science and Technology of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate not later than one year after the date of enactment of this Act.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to international partners and to delivering a plan amount to consultation with outside parties. But the section only directs the NASA Administrator to develop a contingency plan and deliver it to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. Mentioning international partner resupply capabilities as possible content of the plan does not require consulting anyone outside the government before a decision, and there is no comment period, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue.
fable.s: The plan shall be delivered to the Committee on Science and Technology of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate

opus.w: The only process this section sets up is the Administrator writing a plan and sending it to congressional committees. Congress is inside the federal government, so that is not participation. The mention of using international partners' cargo resupply capabilities is about the plan's content, meaning backup supply arrangements. It does not require consulting outside parties, holding a comment period or hearing, or giving anyone a right to object before NASA decides.
opus.s: The plan shall be delivered to the Committee on Science and Technology of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate not later than one year after the date of enactment of this Act.
opus.b: The tempting reading is that "arrangements" using "International Space Station international partner cargo resupply capabilities" means outside parties take part in a federal decision. It doesn't hold up. Those arrangements are about buying or using partners' cargo services as a backup. Nothing says the Administrator must consult the partners, or anyone else outside the federal government, before deciding on the plan. The only formal process is sending the plan to congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Administrator to develop a contingency plan and deliver it to congressional committees. Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to it is not participation. While the plan involves international partners, the statute does not mandate a consultation process, public comment period, or advisory board with outside members to inform the decision; it only mandates the creation and submission of the plan.
qwen_chat.s: The plan shall be delivered to the Committee on Science and Technology of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate not later than one year after the date of enactment of this Act.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "international partner cargo resupply capabilities" implies coordination with foreign governments (outside the federal government). However, the text only mandates the *development* of a plan and its *delivery* to Congress. It does not explicitly require a consultation process, public hearing, or advisory committee involving outsiders *before* the decision is made. The delivery of a report to Congress is explicitly listed as a "No" trap (Congress is inside the federal government). The mention of international partners is descriptive of the plan's content, not a procedural requirement for outside participation in the decision-making process itself.
